one_liner: Paper harness with an AVX-512 header of branch-free double- to quad-double add/multiply that outruns MPFR, QD and CAMPARY.
what_it_does: The repo is the benchmark harness for the SC '25 paper by Zhang and Aiken: one Google Benchmark program per library (GMP mpf, MPFR, CLN, FLINT, libquadmath, Boost.Multiprecision, QD, CAMPARY, MultiFloats) running axpy, dot, gemv and gemm at 1 to 4 doubles of precision. The C++ code you could reuse is multifloats/MultiFloats.hpp, a template MultiFloat<T, N> (N = 1 to 4 limbs, T = double, __m128d, __m256d or __m512d) that only defines operator+ and operator*; there is no subtraction, division, sqrt, comparison, I/O or conversion back to decimal. It is not a drop-in for mpfr_t: precision is fixed at compile time and callers store limbs in separate arrays (y0[], y1[], ...).
how_it_is_fast: Numbers are unevaluated sums of 2 to 4 doubles (floating-point expansions), and each add or multiply is a fixed straight-line network of TwoSum, FastTwoSum and FMA-based TwoProd steps with no branches or renormalization loops (the paper calls these floating-point accumulation networks). With no data-dependent control flow, the same code instantiates on 2-, 4- and 8-wide SIMD registers; the dot and gemv kernels load 8 doubles per limb with _mm512_loadu_pd from split-array (one array per limb) storage, and axpy/gemm rely on '#pragma omp simd simdlen(8)'. The baselines (for example MPFR) are scalar per-element library calls on heap-allocated mpfr_t objects.
when_to_use: Bulk elementwise or BLAS-style kernels (axpy, dot, gemv, small gemm) where double is not accurate enough and roughly 106, 159 or 212 significand bits suffice.
You can lay out data as one double array per limb (structure of arrays) so the add/multiply networks vectorize.
x86-64 with AVX-512 (the harness hardware per the paper abstract snippet was an AMD Ryzen 9 9950X); a scalar ARM header exists for Apple Silicon.
As a reference implementation of the paper's add and multiply networks to port into your own SIMD code, or to reproduce the paper's library comparison (MIT license).
when_not_to_use: You need arbitrary or runtime-selectable precision, correct rounding, or MPFR's exponent range: these types have the exponent range of double and are capped at 4 limbs.

You need anything beyond + and *: the C++ header has no subtraction, division, sqrt, transcendental functions, comparisons or string conversion (the full operation set is in the Julia package MultiFloats.jl).
Your code must handle infinities or NaN-free overflow: TwoSum on an infinite input produces NaN error terms, and the Julia sibling documents that ±Inf inputs return NaN.
Your target CPU lacks AVX-512: the x86 header defines __m512d overloads and uses _mm256_extractf64x2_pd (AVX-512DQ/VL) unconditionally, and the benchmark kernels call _mm512_loadu_pd directly.
You want a maintained library: this is a 2-star benchmark repo with a one-line README and no tests beyond assert checks in the benchmarks.

integration.dependencies: none for MultiFloats.hpp (x86 intrinsics headers only); the harness needs Google Benchmark, OpenMP, GMP, MPFR, CLN, FLINT, Boost.Multiprecision, QD and CAMPARY (fetched by download_campary.sh)
integration.min_toolchain: C++17; the scripts use g++-14 and clang++-20 on Linux and Homebrew LLVM clang++ on macOS
integration.platforms: x86-64 with FMA and AVX-512F/DQ/VL for multifloats/MultiFloats.hpp; multifloats-arm/MultiFloats.hpp is a scalar-only variant (no NEON intrinsics) for aarch64
integration.thread_safety: Value types with no shared state; the benchmark kernels parallelize with OpenMP. Not otherwise documented.

gotchas: The error-free transformations depend on exact IEEE evaluation order: the harness builds with -ffp-contract=off and never enables fast-math; reassociation would cancel the error terms.
Results are not normalized or rounded like MPFR; equality operator== only compares against a scalar double (leading limb equal, lower limbs zero).
The baseline MPFR runs use MPFR_RNDF (faithful rounding) with separate mpfr_mul and mpfr_add calls, so MPFR was not in correctly rounded mode in this harness either.
The repo commits no benchmark output; bench_linux.sh writes Google Benchmark JSON per library at OMP_NUM_THREADS 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1 for you to generate.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick this over DoubleFloats.jl or MPLAPACK's double-double/quad-double backends when you want C++ SIMD kernels at 2 to 4 doubles and can live with only + and *; pick MultiFloats.jl if you work in Julia and need the full operation set, and MPFR-based tools (or LibBF, FLINT) when you need arbitrary precision or correct rounding.
verified_claims_summary: The SC '25 paper abstract (seen only as search snippets; the paper hosts are blocked here) reports peak throughput up to 11.7x QD, 34.4x CAMPARY, 35.6x MPFR and 41.4x FLINT across axpy, dot, gemv and gemm at 2 to 4 doubles, with search snippets naming AMD Zen 5 (Ryzen 9 9950X) and Apple M3 Pro; the public harness builds with g++-14/clang++-20 at -O3 -march=native -flto and runs MPFR at 53, 103, 156 and 208 bits. Which kernel, precision and thread count produce each peak ratio is not documented in the repo.
status_note: Stale research harness (last commit 2025-08-27, 46 commits, 2 stars) under MIT, so the 373-line header is easy to vendor, but it is a paper artifact rather than a supported library.
sources_read: WebSearch: 'High-Performance Branch-Free Algorithms for Extended-Precision Floating-Point Arithmetic' SC25 (abstract snippets; theory.stanford.edu and dl.acm.org not opened)
